title: Do Animals Have Natural Rights?
summary: Part two of a two-part series on animal rights and animal protection. The hosts trace Western views of animal souls from Aristotle's hierarchy of souls through Judeo-Christian dominion, Descartes' 'automaton' view, and Jeremy Bentham's argument that animal suffering matters. They cover the shift from farm life to industrialized meat and the rise of pet keeping, early English anti-cruelty laws (Martin's Act of 1822), Henry Bergh and the ASPCA, the 1966 Animal Welfare Act and its loopholes and 2002 narrowing, and the 1980s amendments after the Head Trauma Center baboon exposé. They then distinguish animal welfare from animal rights, discuss Peter Singer, Tom Regan, and Gary Francione, the militant Animal Liberation Front and Band of Mercy, and Steven Wise's Nonhuman Rights Project seeking legal personhood for chimpanzees. The episode closes with listener mail, including puns and band names.
topics: Tom Regan subject of a life

segments.title: Intro and Aristotle's hierarchy of souls
segments.summary: Hosts introduce part two, plug Primer Stories, and discuss Aristotle's hierarchy of souls placing humans above animals. Banter follows about religious views on animal souls across Judeo-Christian, Mormon, Hindu, Jain, and Jewish traditions, and Descartes' view of animals as automatons.

segments.title: Jeremy Bentham and the question of animal suffering
segments.summary: Hosts describe Jeremy Bentham's argument that the key question is whether animals can suffer, and his felicific calculus. They say he concluded experimentation on animals was morally repugnant.

segments.title: Farm-to-factory shift and pet keeping
segments.summary: Hosts argue that industrialization and the move from farm to city changed how people related to animals, and that pet keeping grew, producing the contradictory view that animals should be protected yet eaten.

segments.title: Early anti-cruelty laws in England and Martin's Act
segments.summary: Hosts describe mid-nineteenth century England, where abuse of animals was legal, and an 1834 Washington, D.C. case of a man charged with a public nuisance for beating a cow. They then cover Lords Erskine and Martin and Martin's Act of 1822, the first Western law criminalizing animal abuse, which covered livestock.

segments.title: Henry Bergh and the ASPCA
segments.summary: Hosts profile Henry Bergh, who founded the ASPCA in New York in 1866 and enforced anti-cruelty rules himself, including breaking up underground bull fights. They note his anecdote from Russia and his support for children's causes kept separate from animal groups. They also discuss the animal cruelty and violence link as a popular belief.

segments.title: Animal Welfare Act and lab animal protections
segments.summary: Hosts cover 1960s stolen-pet stories in Sports Illustrated and Life that aroused the public and led to the 1966 Animal Welfare Act. They describe its coverage limits (excluding rats, mice, birds, and cold-blooded animals), its loose 'unnecessary suffering' standard, the 1970s expansion and 2002 narrowing.

segments.title: Head Trauma Center exposé and amendments
segments.summary: Hosts describe the activist group exposé of a Head Trauma Center lab with baboons, the documentary Unnecessary Fuss, and the resulting amendments requiring lab oversight committees, anesthesia, and postoperative care, with a 'necessary' loophole.

segments.title: Animal welfare versus animal rights
segments.summary: Hosts distinguish the accepted animal welfare view, which allows using animals for food and labor if suffering is avoided, from the animal rights view that animals have inherent moral value and deserve legal rights.

segments.title: Peter Singer, Tom Regan, Gary Francione, and militant activism
segments.summary: Hosts discuss Peter Singer's Animal Liberation, Tom Regan's subjects-of-a-life idea, and Gary Francione's call to abolish animal domination. They describe the Hunt Saboteurs Association, the Band of Mercy's guinea pig raid, and militant tactics by the Animal Liberation Front including threats and fires, as well as PR use of publicity.

segments.title: Legal personhood for animals and Steven Wise
segments.summary: Hosts describe attorney Steven Wise and the Nonhuman Rights Project seeking legal personhood for chimpanzees, including a habeas corpus writ that was reversed the same day, and a Sea World orca case. They raise questions about consequences such as the end of zoos and hunting, and mention guardian laws in some states.
